etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English qualite, from Old French qualité, from Latin quālitās, quālitātem, from quālis (“of what kind”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷo- (“who, how”). Cicero coined qualitas as a calque to translate the Ancient Greek word ποιότης (poiótēs, “quality”), coined by Plato from ποῖος (poîos, “of what nature, of what kind”).

definitions.definition: (archaic) High social position. (See also the quality.)
(uncountable) The degree to which a man-made object or system is free from faults and flaws, as opposed to scope of functions or quantity of items.
(thermodynamics) In a two-phase liquid–vapor mixture, the ratio of the mass of vapor present to the total mass of the mixture.
(emergency medicine, countable) The third step in OPQRST where the responder investigates what the NOI/MOI feels like.
(countable, UK, journalism) A newspaper with relatively serious, high-quality content.

quote.citation: 1998, Bill Coxall, Lynton Robins, Robert Leach, Contemporary British Politics, page 164:
quote.text: It is argued that in the last ten years or so, quality broadsheet newspapers have become more like the tabloids. Anthony Sampson has argued that 'the frontier between the qualities and popular papers has virtually disappeared'.

definitions.definition: (attributive) Being of good worth, well made, fit for purpose; of high quality.
